skills.title: Points, Lines and Segments
skills.summary: The basic objects of geometry and how they are named.
objectives: Name points, lines, rays and segments.
Tell the difference between a line, a ray and a segment.

vocabulary.definition: A piece of a line with two endpoints.
A piece of a line with one endpoint, going on forever the other way.

skills.title: Angles and Their Measure
skills.summary: What an angle is, how it is measured in degrees, and how angles are classified.
objectives: Measure and name angles in degrees.
Classify an angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight.

vocabulary.definition: The unit of angle measure; a full turn is 360 degrees.
An angle smaller than 90 degrees.

skills.title: Angle Relationships
skills.summary: Complementary, supplementary, vertical and adjacent angles.
objectives: Find a missing angle using complementary and supplementary pairs.
Recognise vertical angles as equal.

vocabulary.definition: Two angles that add to 90 degrees.
Two angles that add to 180 degrees.

skills.title: Parallel Lines and Transversals
skills.summary: The equal and supplementary angles formed when a line crosses two parallel lines.
objectives: Identify corresponding and alternate angles.
Find missing angles at a transversal.

vocabulary.definition: A line that crosses two or more other lines.
Always the same distance apart and never meeting.

skills.title: Triangles
skills.summary: Classifying triangles and using the angle sum.
objectives: Classify triangles by their sides and angles.
Find a missing angle in a triangle.

vocabulary.definition: A triangle with two equal sides and two equal angles.
A triangle with all three sides different.

skills.title: Quadrilaterals
skills.summary: Four-sided shapes and the properties that separate them.
objectives: Name quadrilaterals from their properties.
Use the 360 degree angle sum of a quadrilateral.

vocabulary.definition: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.

skills.title: Polygons and Their Angles
skills.summary: Naming polygons and finding their interior angle sums.
objectives: Find the interior angle sum of a polygon.
Find each angle of a regular polygon.

vocabulary.definition: A closed shape made of straight sides.
A polygon with all sides and all angles equal.

skills.title: Perimeter and Area
skills.summary: Distance around a shape and the space it covers.
objectives: Find the perimeter and area of rectangles and triangles.
Find the area of a parallelogram and a trapezoid.

vocabulary.definition: The total distance around the edge of a shape.
The amount of surface a shape covers.

skills.title: Circles
objectives: Convert between radius and diameter.
Find the circumference and area of a circle.

vocabulary.definition: The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
The distance all the way round a circle.

skills.title: Volume and Surface Area
skills.summary: The space inside a solid and the area of its outside.
objectives: Find the volume of a rectangular prism and a cylinder.
Find the surface area of a rectangular prism.

vocabulary.definition: A solid with the same cross-section all the way through.
The total area of all the faces of a solid.

skills.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
skills.summary: The relationship between the sides of a right triangle.
objectives: Find a missing side of a right triangle.
Use the converse to test whether a triangle has a right angle.

vocabulary.definition: The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle.

skills.title: Similarity and Congruence
skills.summary: Shapes that match exactly, and shapes that match in proportion.
objectives: Tell congruent figures from similar ones.
Use a scale factor to find a missing length.

vocabulary.definition: Exactly the same shape and size.
The same shape, with all lengths in the same ratio.

components.body: A point marks a position. A line goes on forever in both directions. A ray starts at a point and goes on forever one way. A segment has two endpoints, so it has a length you can measure.
Segments are named by their endpoints, so the segment from A to B is AB and has the same length as BA.
A segment runs from 3 cm to 11 cm on a ruler. Its length is 11 - 3 = 8 cm.
A ray is not the same as a segment: only one end stops.
Point, line, ray, segment: the difference is how many ends stop.
An angle measures turn. Two rays from the same point open up by some amount, and that amount is the angle.
A full turn is 360 degrees, a half turn is 180 degrees, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees, which is called a right angle.
An angle of 40 degrees is less than 90, so it is acute. An angle of 130 degrees is more than 90 but less than 180, so it is obtuse.
The length of the drawn rays does not change the angle. Only the amount of turn matters.
Acute under 90, right at 90, obtuse between 90 and 180, straight at 180.
Angles that sit together often add to a familiar total. Two angles making a right angle add to 90 degrees. Two angles making a straight line add to 180 degrees.
Angles adding to 90 degrees are complementary; angles adding to 180 degrees are supplementary. When two lines cross, the angles opposite each other are vertical angles and are equal.
If one of two complementary angles is 35 degrees, the other is 90 - 35 = 55 degrees.
Complementary and supplementary are easy to swap. Complementary makes a corner (90); supplementary makes a straight line (180).
Corner pairs make 90, straight-line pairs make 180, and crossed lines give equal opposite angles.
When one line crosses two parallel lines, the crossing looks identical at both. That is why so many of the angles repeat.

Corresponding angles sit in matching positions and are equal. Alternate angles sit on opposite sides of the transversal, between the parallels, and are equal. Co-interior angles are on the same side and add to 180 degrees.
If a corresponding angle is 70 degrees, its partner is also 70 degrees, and the angle next to it on the line is 180 - 70 = 110 degrees.
These rules need the lines to be parallel. Without that, none of the equalities hold.
Matching positions are equal, alternate positions are equal, same-side interior angles add to 180.
Tear the three corners off any paper triangle and put them side by side: they always form a straight line. That is why the angles add to 180 degrees.
By sides: equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (all different). By angles: acute, right or obtuse.
A triangle has angles of 40 and 75 degrees. The third is 180 - 40 - 75 = 65 degrees.
A triangle cannot have two right angles: that alone would use up all 180 degrees.
Three angles, always 180 degrees in total, and equal sides sit opposite equal angles.
Any quadrilateral splits into two triangles, so its angles add to 2 x 180 = 360 degrees.
A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal. A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles. A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. A square is both.
Three angles of a quadrilateral are 100, 80 and 95 degrees. The fourth is 360 - 100 - 80 - 95 = 85 degrees.
Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
Four sides, 360 degrees, and the names describe which sides and angles are equal.
Any polygon can be cut into triangles from one corner. A shape with n sides gives n - 2 triangles.
The interior angles of an n-sided polygon add to (n - 2) x 180 degrees. In a regular polygon every angle is that total divided by n.
A hexagon has 6 sides, so its angles add to (6 - 2) x 180 = 720 degrees. A regular hexagon has angles of 720 / 6 = 120 degrees.
Use n - 2, not n. A quadrilateral gives two triangles, not four.
(n - 2) x 180 for the total; divide by n for each angle when the polygon is regular.
Perimeter is how far you walk round the edge. Area is how many unit squares fit inside.
Rectangle: area = length x width. Triangle: area = half x base x height. Parallelogram: area = base x height. Trapezoid: area = half x (a + b) x height.
A rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm has perimeter 2 x (8 + 5) = 26 cm and area 8 x 5 = 40 square cm.
Adding the sides gives perimeter, not area. Area needs multiplication.
Perimeter adds the edges; area multiplies, and triangles take half.
Every point on a circle is the same distance from the centre. That distance is the radius, and the diameter is twice it.
Circumference = 2 x pi x radius. Area = pi x radius x radius. Take pi as 3.14 unless told otherwise.
A circle of radius 5 cm has circumference 2 x 3.14 x 5 = 31.4 cm and area 3.14 x 25 = 78.5 square cm.
Squaring the diameter instead of the radius makes the area four times too big.
Diameter is twice the radius; circumference uses 2 pi r and area uses pi r squared.
Volume counts the unit cubes that fill a solid. Surface area is the paper you would need to wrap it.
Rectangular prism: volume = length x width x height, surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh). Cylinder: volume = pi x radius x radius x height.
A box 4 by 3 by 2 cm has volume 24 cubic cm and surface area 2(12 + 8 + 6) = 52 square cm.
Volume is measured in cubic units and surface area in square units. Mixing them up is the usual slip.
Volume multiplies three lengths; surface area adds the areas of the faces.
Draw a square on each side of a right triangle. The two smaller squares together have exactly the same area as the largest one.
For a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
Legs of 3 and 4 give 9 + 16 = 25, so the hypotenuse is the square root of 25, which is 5.
The theorem only works for right triangles, and c must be the side opposite the right angle.
a squared plus b squared equals c squared, with c the hypotenuse.
Congruent shapes are copies. Similar shapes are photographs of each other at different sizes: the angles match and every length is scaled by the same factor.
In similar figures, corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in a constant ratio, the scale factor.
A triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is similar to one with sides 6, 8, 10. The scale factor is 2.
Similar shapes do not have equal sides, and congruent shapes are a special case of similar with scale factor 1.
Congruent means identical; similar means the same shape scaled by a constant factor.

questions.prompt: A segment runs from the 4 cm mark to the 13 cm mark on a ruler. How long is it, in centimetres?

hints.text: Length is the distance between the two endpoints.
Subtract the smaller mark from the larger one.

questions.explanation: The segment covers 13 - 4 = 9 cm.

questions.prompt: Which figure has exactly two endpoints?

hints.text: Count how many ends stop.
A ray stops at one end only.

questions.explanation: A segment has two endpoints; a ray has one and a line has none.

questions.prompt: Which figure goes on forever in both directions?

hints.text: Think about which one never stops.
A segment stops at both ends.

questions.explanation: A line extends without end in both directions.

questions.prompt: A segment from the 2 cm mark to the 15 cm mark is divided into two equal parts. How long is each part, in centimetres?

hints.text: First find the whole length.
Then share it equally between two parts.

questions.explanation: The segment is 15 - 2 = 13 cm long, so each half is 13 / 2 = 6.5 cm.

questions.prompt: Point B lies on segment AC. AB is 7 cm and BC is 5 cm. How long is AC, in centimetres?

hints.text: B is between A and C, so the two shorter pieces make the whole.
Add the two pieces.

questions.explanation: AC = AB + BC = 7 + 5 = 12 cm.

questions.prompt: Point M is the midpoint of segment PQ, which is 24 cm long. How long is PM, in centimetres?

hints.text: A midpoint splits a segment into two equal pieces.
Halve the total length.

questions.explanation: The midpoint halves the segment, so PM = 24 / 2 = 12 cm.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

correct_answer: A segment has a measurable length.
A ray has exactly one endpoint.

hints.text: Check each statement against the definitions.
Only figures with two stopping ends have a length.

questions.explanation: A segment has two endpoints and a measurable length; a ray has one endpoint and no length.

options: A segment has a measurable length.
A ray has exactly one endpoint.
A line has a measurable length.
A point has a length of zero centimetres.

questions.prompt: A fence post sits every 3 m along a straight 21 m fence, including one at each end. How many posts are there?

hints.text: Work out how many gaps of 3 m fit into 21 m.
There is always one more post than there are gaps.

questions.explanation: There are 21 / 3 = 7 gaps, and one more post than gaps, so 8 posts.

questions.prompt: How many degrees are there in a right angle?

hints.text: A right angle is a quarter of a full turn.
A full turn is 360 degrees.

questions.explanation: A right angle is a quarter turn, and 360 / 4 = 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: How many degrees are there in a straight angle?

hints.text: A straight angle is a half turn.
Half of 360 is what you need.

questions.explanation: A straight angle is half a full turn, so it is 360 / 2 = 180 degrees.

questions.prompt: An angle measures 35 degrees. What kind of angle is it?

hints.text: Compare it with 90 degrees.
Angles below 90 degrees are acute.

questions.explanation: 35 degrees is less than 90 degrees, so the angle is acute.

questions.prompt: An angle measures 118 degrees. What kind of angle is it?

hints.text: It is bigger than a right angle.
Obtuse angles lie between 90 and 180 degrees.

questions.explanation: 118 degrees is more than 90 but less than 180, so the angle is obtuse.

questions.prompt: A turn of one quarter is followed by another quarter turn in the same direction. How many degrees is the total turn?

hints.text: Each quarter turn is 90 degrees.
Add the two turns together.

questions.explanation: Two quarter turns are 90 + 90 = 180 degrees, a straight angle.

questions.prompt: A clock's minute hand moves from 12 to 3. Through how many degrees has it turned?

hints.text: A full circuit of the clock face is 360 degrees.
From 12 to 3 is a quarter of the way round.

questions.explanation: 12 to 3 is a quarter of the face, so the hand turns 360 / 4 = 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: Put these angles in order from smallest to largest.

hints.text: Compare the numbers of degrees.
Smallest first.

questions.explanation: Ordered by size: 15, 88, 90, then 140 degrees.

questions.prompt: A wheel turns through 720 degrees. How many complete turns is that?

hints.text: One complete turn is 360 degrees.
Divide the total by 360.

questions.explanation: 720 / 360 = 2 complete turns.

questions.prompt: Two complementary angles are shown. One measures 35 degrees. How many degrees is the other?

hints.text: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees.
Subtract 35 from 90.

questions.explanation: Complementary angles add to 90, so the other angle is 90 - 35 = 55 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two complementary angles are shown. One measures 62 degrees. How many degrees is the other?

hints.text: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees.
Subtract 62 from 90.

questions.explanation: Complementary angles add to 90, so the other angle is 90 - 62 = 28 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two supplementary angles are shown. One measures 110 degrees. How many degrees is the other?

hints.text: Supplementary angles add to 180 degrees.
Subtract 110 from 180.

questions.explanation: Supplementary angles add to 180, so the other angle is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two supplementary angles are shown. One measures 75 degrees. How many degrees is the other?

hints.text: Supplementary angles add to 180 degrees.
Subtract 75 from 180.

questions.explanation: Supplementary angles add to 180, so the other angle is 180 - 75 = 105 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles measures 47 degrees. How many degrees is the angle vertically opposite it?

hints.text: Vertical angles are the ones directly opposite each other.
Vertically opposite angles are always equal.

questions.explanation: Vertical angles are equal, so the opposite angle is also 47 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle measures 47 degrees. How many degrees is the angle next to it on the straight line?

hints.text: Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees.
Subtract 47 from 180.

questions.explanation: The two angles form a straight line, so the neighbour is 180 - 47 = 133 degrees.

questions.prompt: Three angles meet at a point on one side of a straight line. Two of them are 55 degrees and 68 degrees. How many degrees is the third?

hints.text: Angles along a straight line add to 180 degrees.
Subtract both known angles from 180.

questions.prompt: An angle is twice the size of its complement. How many degrees is the larger angle?

hints.text: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees.
If the smaller is x, the larger is 2x, and x + 2x = 90.

questions.explanation: With x + 2x = 90, x = 30, so the larger angle is 2 x 30 = 60 degrees.

questions.prompt: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One angle measures 70 degrees. How many degrees is the corresponding angle?

hints.text: Corresponding angles sit in matching positions at each crossing.
Corresponding angles are equal.

questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal, so the answer is 70 degrees.

questions.prompt: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. An alternate interior angle to a 65 degree angle is shown. How many degrees is it?

hints.text: Alternate angles lie on opposite sides of the transversal.
Alternate interior angles are equal.

questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal, so it is 65 degrees.

questions.prompt: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One co-interior angle is 110 degrees. How many degrees is the other?

hints.text: Co-interior angles are on the same side of the transversal.
They add to 180 degrees.

questions.explanation: Co-interior angles add to 180, so the other is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees.

questions.prompt: Which pair of angles is always equal when a transversal crosses two parallel lines?

hints.text: Think about which angles sit in matching positions.
Co-interior angles add to 180 rather than being equal.

questions.explanation: Corresponding angles occupy matching positions at each crossing and are equal.

questions.prompt: A transversal makes an angle of 42 degrees with the first of two parallel lines. How many degrees is the obtuse angle at the second line?

hints.text: The acute angle repeats at the second crossing.
The obtuse angle completes a straight line with it.

questions.explanation: The acute angle is 42 degrees at both crossings, so the obtuse angle is 180 - 42 = 138 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two lines are crossed by a transversal. The corresponding angles measure 80 degrees and 85 degrees. What can you conclude?

hints.text: Corresponding angles are equal only when the lines are parallel.
Here they are not equal.

questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal exactly when the lines are parallel, and 80 is not 85, so the lines are not parallel.

questions.prompt: Select every angle pair that is equal when a transversal crosses parallel lines.

hints.text: Three of these are equal pairs.
Co-interior angles add to 180 instead.

questions.explanation: Corresponding, alternate interior and vertical angles are all equal; co-interior angles are supplementary.

questions.prompt: A ladder leans against a wall, making a 65 degree angle with the level ground. The wall is vertical. How many degrees is the angle between the ladder and the wall?

hints.text: The wall and the ground meet at a right angle.
The three angles of the triangle add to 180.

questions.explanation: The ground-wall angle is 90 degrees, so the ladder-wall angle is 180 - 90 - 65 = 25 degrees.

questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle measure 40 degrees and 75 degrees. How many degrees is the third?

hints.text: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.
Work out 180 - 40 - 75.

questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle measure 90 degrees and 35 degrees. How many degrees is the third?

hints.text: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.
Work out 180 - 90 - 35.

questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle measure 60 degrees and 60 degrees. How many degrees is the third?

hints.text: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.
Work out 180 - 60 - 60.

questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle measure 25 degrees and 110 degrees. How many degrees is the third?

hints.text: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.

questions.prompt: A triangle has three equal sides. What is it called?

hints.text: Think about what the sides tell you.
All three sides equal has its own name.

questions.explanation: A triangle with three equal sides is equilateral, and its angles are all 60 degrees.

questions.prompt: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40 degrees. How many degrees is each base angle?

hints.text: The two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
Subtract 40 from 180, then halve what is left.

questions.explanation: The base angles share 180 - 40 = 140 degrees equally, so each is 70 degrees.

questions.prompt: Can a triangle have two right angles?

hints.text: Add two right angles together.
Compare that with the 180 degree total.

questions.explanation: Two right angles already total 180 degrees, leaving nothing for the third angle, so it is impossible.

questions.prompt: A triangular sail has angles in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. How many degrees is the largest angle?

hints.text: The ratio parts add to 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
Share 180 degrees into 6 parts, then take 3 of them.

questions.explanation: Each part is 180 / 6 = 30 degrees, so the largest angle is 3 x 30 = 90 degrees.

questions.prompt: How many degrees do the four angles of a quadrilateral add to?

hints.text: Split the shape into two triangles.
Each triangle contributes 180 degrees.

questions.explanation: A quadrilateral splits into two triangles, so 2 x 180 = 360 degrees.

questions.prompt: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 100, 80 and 95 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth?

hints.text: The four angles add to 360 degrees.
Subtract the three known angles from 360.

questions.prompt: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 90, 90 and 60 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth?

hints.text: The four angles add to 360 degrees.
Subtract the three known angles from 360.

questions.prompt: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 120, 65 and 100 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth?

hints.text: The four angles add to 360 degrees.
Subtract the three known angles from 360.

questions.prompt: Which shape always has four equal sides and four right angles?

hints.text: It needs both equal sides and right angles.
A rhombus has equal sides but not always right angles.

questions.explanation: A square has four equal sides and four right angles.

questions.prompt: Is every rectangle a square?

hints.text: A square needs all four sides equal.
A rectangle only needs opposite sides equal.

questions.explanation: A rectangle needs right angles but not equal sides, so a 3 by 5 rectangle is not a square.

options: Only if it is a parallelogram

questions.prompt: Select every shape that always has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

hints.text: Check the definition of a parallelogram.
A trapezoid has only one pair of parallel sides.

questions.explanation: Squares, rectangles and rhombuses are all parallelograms; a trapezoid has just one parallel pair.

questions.prompt: A kite-shaped garden bed has two angles of 95 degrees each and a third of 60 degrees. How many degrees is the fourth angle?

hints.text: The angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees.
Subtract all three known angles.

questions.prompt: How many degrees do the interior angles of a pentagon (5 sides) add to?

hints.text: A polygon with n sides splits into n - 2 triangles.
Work out (5 - 2) x 180.

questions.prompt: How many degrees do the interior angles of a hexagon (6 sides) add to?

hints.text: A polygon with n sides splits into n - 2 triangles.
Work out (6 - 2) x 180.

questions.prompt: How many degrees do the interior angles of a octagon (8 sides) add to?

hints.text: A polygon with n sides splits into n - 2 triangles.
Work out (8 - 2) x 180.

questions.prompt: How many degrees is each interior angle of a regular hexagon (6 sides)?

hints.text: First find the total: (6 - 2) x 180.
Then share it equally between 6 angles.

questions.explanation: The total is 720 degrees, so each angle is 720 / 6 = 120 degrees.

questions.prompt: How many degrees is each interior angle of a regular pentagon (5 sides)?

hints.text: First find the total: (5 - 2) x 180.
Then share it equally between 5 angles.

questions.explanation: The total is 540 degrees, so each angle is 540 / 5 = 108 degrees.

questions.prompt: A polygon's interior angles add to 900 degrees. How many sides does it have?

hints.text: Divide 900 by 180 first, then add 2.

questions.explanation: 900 / 180 = 5, so n - 2 = 5 and n = 7 sides.

questions.prompt: What is a polygon with all sides and all angles equal called?

hints.text: The name describes evenness.
It applies to both sides and angles.

questions.explanation: A polygon with equal sides and equal angles is called regular.

questions.prompt: A floor is tiled with regular hexagons meeting at a point. How many degrees do the angles at that point add to?

hints.text: Tiles meeting at a point fill a complete turn.
A complete turn is 360 degrees.

questions.explanation: Angles round a point always total 360 degrees, which is why three 120 degree hexagon angles fit exactly.

questions.prompt: A rectangle measures 8 cm by 5 cm. What is its perimeter, in centimetres?

hints.text: Perimeter is the total distance round the edge.
Add all four sides, or use 2 x (length + width).

questions.prompt: A rectangle measures 8 cm by 5 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: Area counts the unit squares that fit inside.
Multiply length by width.

questions.explanation: 8 x 5 = 40 square cm.

questions.prompt: A triangle has a base of 12 cm and a height of 7 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: A triangle is half of a rectangle with the same base and height.
Work out half of base x height.

questions.explanation: Half of 12 x 7 = 84 gives an area of 42 square cm.

questions.prompt: A parallelogram has a base of 9 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: Use the perpendicular height, not the slanted side.
Area is base x height.

questions.explanation: 9 x 4 = 36 square cm.

questions.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel sides of 6 cm and 10 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: Average the two parallel sides first.
Then multiply by the height.

questions.explanation: Half of (6 + 10) is 8, and 8 x 5 = 40 square cm.

questions.prompt: A square has a perimeter of 36 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: A square has four equal sides, so find one side first.
Then multiply the side by itself.

questions.explanation: Each side is 36 / 4 = 9 cm, so the area is 9 x 9 = 81 square cm.

questions.prompt: A rectangular room is 5 m long and 4 m wide. Carpet costs 12 pounds per square metre. What is the total cost, in pounds?

hints.text: Find the floor area first.
Then multiply the area by the price per square metre.

questions.explanation: The area is 5 x 4 = 20 square metres, so the cost is 20 x 12 = 240 pounds.

questions.prompt: Two rectangles both have an area of 24 square cm. Must they have the same perimeter?

hints.text: Try 4 by 6 and 2 by 12.
Work out both perimeters and compare.

questions.explanation: A 4 by 6 rectangle has perimeter 20 cm and a 2 by 12 rectangle has perimeter 28 cm, so equal areas need not mean equal perimeters.

options: Only if the sides are whole numbers

questions.prompt: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. What is its diameter, in centimetres?

hints.text: The diameter passes through the centre.
It is twice the radius.

questions.explanation: The diameter is 2 x 7 = 14 cm.

questions.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 18 cm. What is its radius, in centimetres?

hints.text: The radius is half the diameter.
Halve 18.

questions.explanation: The radius is 18 / 2 = 9 cm.

questions.prompt: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. What is its circumference, in centimetres? Use pi = 3.14.

hints.text: Circumference is 2 x pi x radius.
Work out 2 x 3.14 x 5.

questions.prompt: A circle has a radius of 5 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres? Use pi = 3.14.

hints.text: Area is pi x radius x radius.
Square the radius first, then multiply by 3.14.

questions.explanation: 5 x 5 = 25 and 3.14 x 25 = 78.5 square cm.

questions.prompt: A circle has a diameter of 20 cm. What is its circumference, in centimetres? Use pi = 3.14.

hints.text: Circumference is pi x diameter.
Work out 3.14 x 20.

questions.prompt: A circular tabletop has a radius of 60 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres? Use pi = 3.14.

hints.text: Square the radius first.
60 x 60 = 3600, then multiply by 3.14.

questions.prompt: If the radius of a circle doubles, what happens to its area?

answer_spec.correct_answer: It becomes four times as large.

hints.text: Area depends on the radius squared.
Doubling and then squaring multiplies by 4.

questions.explanation: Area uses the radius squared, so doubling the radius multiplies the area by 2 x 2 = 4.

options: It becomes four times as large.
It becomes eight times as large.

questions.prompt: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. How far does it travel in one full turn, in centimetres? Use pi = 3.14.

hints.text: One full turn covers the circumference.
Circumference is pi x diameter.

questions.explanation: 3.14 x 70 = 219.8 cm in one turn.

questions.prompt: A box measures 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. What is its volume, in cubic centimetres?

hints.text: Volume counts the unit cubes inside.
Multiply all three dimensions.

questions.explanation: 4 x 3 x 2 = 24 cubic cm.

questions.prompt: A box measures 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. What is its surface area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: There are three different pairs of faces.
Add the three face areas, then double.

questions.explanation: 2 x (12 + 8 + 6) = 52 square cm.

questions.prompt: A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its volume, in cubic centimetres?

hints.text: All edges of a cube are equal.
Multiply the edge by itself three times.

questions.explanation: 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 cubic cm.

questions.prompt: A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its surface area, in square centimetres?

hints.text: A cube has six identical square faces.
Find one face area, then multiply by 6.

questions.explanation: Each face is 5 x 5 = 25, so the surface area is 6 x 25 = 150 square cm.

questions.prompt: A cylinder has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 10 cm. What is its volume, in cubic centimetres? Use pi = 3.14.

hints.text: Find the area of the circular base first.
Then multiply by the height.

questions.explanation: The base area is 3.14 x 9 = 28.26, and 28.26 x 10 = 282.6 cubic cm.

questions.prompt: Which unit is correct for a volume?

hints.text: Volume fills space in three directions.
Square units measure a flat surface.

questions.explanation: Volume is measured in cubic units, because three lengths are multiplied together.

questions.prompt: A fish tank measures 60 cm by 30 cm by 40 cm. What is its volume, in cubic centimetres?

hints.text: Multiply the three dimensions.
60 x 30 = 1800, then multiply by 40.

questions.explanation: 60 x 30 x 40 = 72000 cubic cm.

questions.prompt: If every edge of a cube is doubled, what happens to its volume?

answer_spec.correct_answer: It becomes eight times as large.

hints.text: Volume multiplies three lengths.
Doubling each of three dimensions multiplies by 2 x 2 x 2.

questions.explanation: Each of the three dimensions doubles, so the volume is multiplied by 8.

options: It becomes eight times as large.
It becomes four times as large.
It becomes six times as large.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 3 cm and 4 cm. How long is the hypotenuse, in centimetres?

hints.text: Square both legs and add them.
3 squared is 9 and 4 squared is 16; take the square root of the total.

questions.explanation: 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5 cm.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the hypotenuse, in centimetres?

hints.text: Square both legs and add them.
6 squared is 36 and 8 squared is 64; take the square root of the total.

questions.explanation: 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10 cm.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 5 cm and 12 cm. How long is the hypotenuse, in centimetres?

hints.text: Square both legs and add them.
5 squared is 25 and 12 squared is 144; take the square root of the total.

questions.explanation: 25 + 144 = 169, and the square root of 169 is 13 cm.

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides of 8, 15 and 17. Is it a right triangle?

hints.text: Test the two shorter sides against the longest.
Check whether 64 + 225 equals 289.

questions.explanation: 8 squared plus 15 squared is 64 + 225 = 289, which is 17 squared, so it is a right triangle.

questions.prompt: A ladder 13 m long leans against a wall with its foot 5 m from the base. How far up the wall does it reach, in metres?

hints.text: The wall, ground and ladder form a right triangle.
The ladder is the hypotenuse: 169 - 25 = 144.

questions.explanation: 13 squared minus 5 squared is 169 - 25 = 144, and the square root of 144 is 12 m.

questions.prompt: In a right triangle, which side is always the longest?

hints.text: It sits opposite the right angle.
The largest angle faces the longest side.

questions.explanation: The hypotenuse lies opposite the right angle, the largest angle, so it is always the longest side.

questions.prompt: Two triangles have exactly the same shape and size. What are they called?

hints.text: Same shape and same size.
Similar allows a size change.

questions.explanation: Figures that match exactly in both shape and size are congruent.

questions.prompt: A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 is enlarged to one with sides 6, 8 and 10. What is the scale factor?

hints.text: Compare a pair of matching sides.
Divide a new length by the matching old one.

questions.explanation: 6 / 3 = 2, and the same factor works for the other sides, so the scale factor is 2.

questions.prompt: Two similar rectangles have a scale factor of 3. The smaller is 4 cm wide. How wide is the larger, in centimetres?

hints.text: Every length multiplies by the scale factor.
Work out 4 x 3.

questions.prompt: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides of 5 cm and 15 cm. Another side of the smaller triangle is 7 cm. How long is the matching side of the larger, in centimetres?

hints.text: Find the scale factor from the pair you know: 15 / 5.
Apply that factor to the 7 cm side.

questions.explanation: The scale factor is 15 / 5 = 3, so the matching side is 7 x 3 = 21 cm.

questions.prompt: In two similar figures, what is true of corresponding angles?

hints.text: Similar figures have the same shape.
Only the lengths change under scaling.

questions.explanation: Scaling changes lengths but never angles, so corresponding angles in similar figures are equal.

options: They are in the same ratio as the sides.

questions.prompt: A photograph 10 cm wide and 15 cm tall is enlarged so that it is 25 cm wide. How tall is it, in centimetres?

hints.text: Find the scale factor: 25 / 10 = 2.5.
Multiply the height by that factor.

questions.explanation: The scale factor is 25 / 10 = 2.5, so the height becomes 15 x 2.5 = 37.5 cm.

questions.prompt: Are all squares similar to one another?

hints.text: Every square has four right angles and four equal sides.
Ask whether one can always be scaled to another.

questions.explanation: Every square has the same angles and equal sides, so any square scales onto any other. All squares are similar.

options: Only if the sides are whole numbers

questions.prompt: A 2 m stick casts a 3 m shadow. At the same moment a tree casts a 24 m shadow. How tall is the tree, in metres?

hints.text: The stick and the tree make similar triangles with their shadows.
Height / shadow is the same for both: 2 / 3 = h / 24.

questions.explanation: The ratio of height to shadow is 2 / 3, so the tree is 24 x 2 / 3 = 16 m tall.
